exampleAnswers.title: Checking Whether a Given Function Is a Valid PDF

question.text:
\[ f(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{2}{x^3}, \quad & x \geq 1,\\[5pt] 0, \quad &\textrm{otherwise.} \end{cases} \]

Given the function $f(x)$ above, which of the following statements are true?

  1. $f(x) \geq 0$ for all $x \geq 1$
  2. $\displaystyle \int_{1}^{\infty} f(x) \,\textrm{d}x = 1$
  3. $f(x)$ is a valid probability density function
question.explanation:
For a function $f(x)$ to be a valid probability density function on a set $S,$ it must satisfy the following conditions:

  • $f(x) \geq 0$ for all $x \in S$

  • $\displaystyle \int_{S} f(x) \, \textrm dx = 1$

Now, let's consider each statement in turn:

  • Statement I is true. Indeed, for $x \geq 1,$ we have $f(x) = \dfrac{2}{x^3} \geq 0.$

  • Statement II is true. Indeed, \begin{align} \int_{1}^{\infty} f(x) \,\textrm{d}x & = \int_{1}^{\infty} \dfrac{2}{x^3} \,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = -\dfrac{1}{x^2} \, \Bigg|_{1}^{\infty} \\[5pt] & = -\left(0 - 1\right) \\[5pt] & = 1 \end{align}

  • Statement III is true. Since statements I and II are true, the first and second conditions are satisfied. So, $f(x)$ is a valid probability density function.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

question.text:
\[ f(x) = \begin{cases} 2e^{2x}, \quad & x \leq 0,\\[5pt] 0, \quad &\textrm{otherwise.} \end{cases} \]

Given the function $f(x)$ above, which of the following statements are true?

  1. $f(x) \geq 0$ for all $x \leq 0$
  2. $\displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^{0} f(x) \,\textrm{d}x = 1$
  3. $f(x)$ is a valid probability density function
question.explanation:
For a function $f(x)$ to be a valid probability density function on a set $S,$ it must satisfy the following conditions:

  • $f(x) \geq 0$ for all $x \in S$

  • $\displaystyle \int_{S} f(x) \, \textrm dx = 1$

Now, let's consider each statement in turn:

  • Statement I is true. Indeed, for $x \leq 0,$ we have $f(x) = 2e^{2x} \geq 0.$

  • Statement II is true. Indeed, \begin{align} \int_{-\infty}^{0} f(x) \,\textrm{d}x & = \int_{-\infty}^{0} 2e^{2x} \,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = e^{2x} \, \Big|_{-\infty}^{0} \\[5pt] & = e^0 - 0\\[5pt] & = 1 \end{align}

  • Statement III is true. Since statements I and II are true, the first and second conditions are satisfied. So, $f(x)$ is a valid probability density function.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

exampleAnswers.title: Solving for a Constant Given a PDF

question.text: Solve for $k$ given that the following function is a probability density function: \[ f(x) = \begin{cases}ke^{10x}, \quad & x \lt 0,\\0, \quad &\textrm{otherwise.}\end{cases} \]
question.explanation:
For a function $f(x)$ defined on a set $S$ to be a valid probability density function, it must satisfy the following conditions:

  • $f(x) \geq 0$ for all $x \in S$

  • $\displaystyle \int_{S} f(x) \, \textrm dx = 1$

In our case, for the function $f(x) = ke^{10x}$ on the interval $-\infty < x < 0,$ the second condition states that

\[ \int_{-\infty}^0 ke^{10x} \, \textrm dx = 1. \]

Computing the integral on the left-hand side, we get

\[\begin{align*} \int_{-\infty}^0 ke^{10x} \, \textrm dx = \left[ \dfrac{k}{10}e^{10x} \right]_{-\infty}^0 = \dfrac{k}{10}. \end{align*}\]

Substituting this result back into the first equation and solving for $k,$ we get

\[ \dfrac{k}{10} = 1 \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad k = 10. \]

question.text: Solve for $k$ given that the following function is a probability density function: \[ f(x) = \begin{cases}ke^{-5x}, \quad & x \geq 0,\\0, \quad &\textrm{otherwise.}\end{cases} \]
question.explanation:
For a function $f(x)$ defined on a set $S$ to be a valid probability density function, it must satisfy the following conditions:

  • $f(x) \geq 0$ for all $x \in S$

  • $\displaystyle \int_{S} f(x) \, \textrm dx = 1$

In our case, for the function $f(x) = ke^{-5x}$ on the interval $0 \leq x < \infty,$ the second condition states that

\[ \int_0^{\infty} ke^{-5x} \, \textrm dx = 1. \]

Computing the integral on the left-hand side, we get

\[\begin{align*} \int_0^{\infty} ke^{-5x} \, \textrm dx = \left[ -\dfrac{k}{5}e^{-5x} \right]_0^{\infty} = \dfrac{k}{5}. \end{align*}\]

Substituting this result back into the first equation and solving for $k,$ we get

\[ \dfrac{k}{5} = 1 \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad k = 5. \]

question.text: Solve for $k$ given that the following function is a probability density function: \[ f(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{k}{(2x-1)^2}, \quad & x \geq 2,\\[5pt] 0, \quad &\textrm{otherwise.} \end{cases} \]
question.explanation:
For a function $f(x)$ defined on a set $S$ to be a valid probability density function, it must satisfy the following conditions:

  • $f(x) \geq 0$ for all $x \in S$

  • $\displaystyle \int_{S} f(x) \, \textrm dx = 1$

In our case, for the function $f(x) = \dfrac{k}{(2x-1)^2}$ on the interval $x \geq 2,$ the second condition states that \[ \int_{2}^{\infty} \dfrac{k}{(2x-1)^2} \, \textrm dx = 1. \]

Computing the integral on the left-hand side, we get \begin{align*} \int_{2}^{\infty} \dfrac{k}{(2x-1)^2} \, \textrm dx = -\dfrac{k}{2(2x-1)} \, \Bigg|_{2}^{\infty} = \dfrac{k}{6}. \end{align*}

Substituting this result back into the first equation and solving for $k,$ we get \[ \dfrac{k}{6} = 1 \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad k = 6. \]

question.text: Solve for $k$ given that the following function is a probability density function: \[ f(x) = \begin{cases} ke^{2-x}, \quad & x \geq -1,\\[5pt] 0, \quad &\textrm{otherwise.} \end{cases} \]
question.explanation:
For a function $f(x)$ defined on a set $S$ to be a valid probability density function, it must satisfy the following conditions:

  • $f(x) \geq 0$ for all $x \in S$

  • $\displaystyle \int_{S} f(x) \, \textrm dx = 1$

In our case, for the function $f(x) = ke^{2-x}$ on the interval $x \geq -1,$ the second condition states that \[ \int_{-1}^{\infty} ke^{2-x} \, \textrm dx = 1. \]

Computing the integral on the left-hand side, we get \begin{align*} \int_{-1}^{\infty} ke^{2-x} \, \textrm dx = -ke^{2-x} \, \Bigg|_{-1}^{\infty} = ke^{3}. \end{align*}

Substituting this result back into the first equation and solving for $k,$ we get \[ k e^3 = 1 \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad k = e^{-3}. \]

question.text: Solve for $k$ given that the following function is a probability density function: \[ f(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{k}{(4-x)^3}, \quad & x \leq 2,\\[5pt] 0, \quad &\textrm{otherwise.} \end{cases} \]
question.explanation:
For a function $f(x)$ defined on a set $S$ to be a valid probability density function, it must satisfy the following conditions:

  • $f(x) \geq 0$ for all $x \in S$

  • $\displaystyle \int_{S} f(x) \, \textrm dx = 1$

In our case, for the function $f(x) = \dfrac{k}{(4-x)^3}$ on the interval $x \leq 2,$ the second condition states that \[ \int_{-\infty}^{2} \dfrac{k}{(4-x)^3} \, \textrm dx = 1. \]

Computing the integral on the left-hand side, we get \begin{align*} \int_{-\infty}^{2} \dfrac{k}{(4-x)^3} \, \textrm dx = \dfrac{k}{2(4-x)^2} \, \Bigg|_{-\infty}^{2} = \dfrac{k}{8}. \end{align*}

Substituting this result back into the first equation and solving for $k,$ we get \[ \dfrac{k}{8} = 1 \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad k = 8. \]

exampleAnswers.title: Computing a Probability Over an Unbounded Interval

question.text:
Compute $P\left( X > 8 \right)$ given that the random variable $X$ has the probability density function

\[ f(x) = \begin{cases}\dfrac{3}{x^2}, \quad &x \geq 3,\\0, \quad &x< 3.\end{cases} \]
question.explanation:
If a continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function $f(x),$ then \[ P(a < X < b) = \int_a^b f(x) \, \textrm dx. \]

So, in our case, we have

\[\begin{align*} P( X > 8 ) &= P(8 < X < \infty) \\[5pt] &= \int_8^\infty f(x) \, \textrm dx \\[5pt] &= \int_8^\infty \dfrac{3}{x^2} \, \textrm dx \\[5pt] &= \left[ - \dfrac{3}{x} \right]_8^\infty \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{8}. \end{align*}\]

question.text:
Compute $P\left( X \leq -5 \right)$ given that the random variable $X$ has the probability density function

\[ f(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{3}{x^2}, \quad &x \leq -3, \\ 0, \quad &x \gt -3.\end{cases} \]
question.explanation:
If a continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function $f(x),$ then \[ P(a < X < b) = \int_a^b f(x) \, \textrm dx. \]

So, in our case, we have

\[\begin{align*} P( X \leq -5 ) &= P(-\infty < X \leq -5) \\[5pt] &= \int_{-\infty}^{-5} f(x) \, \textrm dx \\[5pt] &= \int_{-\infty}^{-5} \dfrac{3}{x^2} \, \textrm dx \\[5pt] &= \left[ - \dfrac{3}{x} \right]_{-\infty}^{-5} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{5}. \end{align*}\]

If a continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function $f(x),$ then \[ P(a < X < b) = \int_a^b f(x) \, \textrm dx. \]

So, in our case, we have
